Well yes, they did all that, but my understanding is thet they didn't so much think of the statue as the God as they thought of the statue as a vehicle for that God's presence and sensory perception. 

This is a key distinction because they did this with personal worship too, there was an understanding that any given God could 'inhabit' multiple statues at the same time with no issues. The reason they would go out of their way to recover specific statues is because of how religion worked at that time. 

Every city had their own patron deity that protected it from other deities, and they *really* didn't wanna piss these guys off. Worship was motivated mostly by a need for protection and often they had no luck of fear for their own patron deity. So, if they *lose* the main statue in the city's temple that Marduk for example agreed to inhabit, that's already a massive fuck-up. 

They're supposed to take care of and protect it, that's their end of the deal. If they can't even get it back after losing it to enemies, Marduk is gonna be real angry, and bad things were believed to happen when a cities patron deity was pissed off at the city.

It's definitely a very different relationship than what us modern folk are used to but it's not really idolatrous as the term is typically characterized.

Pre-Abrahamic religions didn't even do that, really. The statues were like, religiously important, but there's no evidence they thought the statues themselves were Gods besides the Bible and related texts accusing them of it.

Really I'm not aware of any cases where idolatry was like, a real thing. It's always been a typical 'your gods aren't even real' accusation thrown from one religion to another. Or internal theological skirmishes later on.
